newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's old rulers back arms sales to China.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's old rulers back arms sales to China.

text.p: South Africa's former white rulers said on Tuesday they would support future arms sales to China but reiterated their opposition to any deals with Syria.

The National Party, prompted by a South African radar company's confirmation that a delegation from Beijing had visited Johannesburg last year to investigate a possible contract, said trade with China would not isolate Pretoria.

"In contrast to the Syrian case, China does not appear on any blacklists with regard to the provision of arms, and some of the most important Western countries sell arms to China," NP foreign affairs spokesman Boy Geldenhuys said in a statement.
"Except for raw materials, arms are South Africa's biggest export...It is essential for the arms industry for South Africa to compete on the world market," he added.

The National Party's relations with Taiwan date back to the apartheid era when both were diplomatic pariahs. President Nelson Mandela announced in late 1996 that the country would switch recognition to Beijing from Taipei by the end of 1997.

The South African firm, Reutech Radar Systems, said on Monday reports it was negotiating a one billion rand ($220 million) arms sale to China were overblown, but revealed that Beijing had sent a delegation to the country in May last year.
Reutech said the delegation had assessed a highly mobile two-dimensional radar system which it had developed in cooperation with the government-controlled Armscor agency.

Last month, the South African cabinet deferred a final decision over a proposed sale of tank firing and guidance systems to Syria to improve and modernise the targeting ability of its Soviet-built T-72 tanks.

The proposed sale became a foreign policy wrangle, with the United States threatening to cut off aid to South Africa if it went ahead with the deal. Washington regards Damascus as a state sponsor of terrorism -- a charge Syria denies.
